data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A decentralized network of small, independently operated services is only more resilient to correlated failure than one large service if the decentralized nodes lack shared upstream dependencies; otherwise, their independence is an illusion masking a latent common-cause failure mode.","counterconditions":[{"case":"Decentralized nodes are proven to have no shared upstream dependencies, making their failures truly independent.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The large service's internal redundancy includes independent replicas of all external dependencies, achieving strict isolation.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"Empirical data shows decentralized nodes fail at statistically independent rates under all observed perturbations, including upstream outages.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Decentralized services appear independent because they fail at different times and for different apparent reasons under normal conditions. However, if they share common upstream dependencies (e.g., a cloud provider, DNS registrar, certificate authority, or core library), then a single failure in that dependency will cascade across all services simultaneously. The large service, despite having strictly more total internal redundancy, can be designed to tolerate internal component failures, but neither architecture can withstand the loss of a shared external dependency. Therefore, resilience to correlated failure depends on eliminating shared upstream dependencies, not merely on distributing the services.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
